Who sets and collects property tax

Property tax in Massachusetts is a town-by-town matter. All 351 cities and towns assess and collect it themselves, which means your bill is set by the municipality and not the county. The Division of Local Services, part of the Department of Revenue, oversees the system, and your local board of assessors holds the property record card for your house.

Value is set as of January 1 for the fiscal year that follows. Fiscal year 2025, for example, runs July 1, 2024 to June 30, 2025, and its valuation date is January 1, 2024. That gap explains why a bill can reflect a value set well before you list the house.

Proposition 2½ and your bill

Proposition 2½ limits what a city or town can raise in total, not what any single owner pays. There are two restrictions: the levy cannot exceed 2.5% of the community's total assessed value, and the yearly increase is capped at 2.5% of the prior year's levy limit plus new growth.

Voters can go above that only through an override, a debt exclusion or a capital exclusion.

Your own bill can still change, since the whole levy gets split across every taxable parcel. If neighboring values climb faster than yours, you may pay a smaller share even as your value goes up.

Due dates

How often you pay depends on your town. Quarterly towns usually collect on four dates a year. Towns that bill twice a year give you about 30 days from the mailing date.

Billing styleGeneral due dates
QuarterlyAugust 1, November 1, February 1, May 1
Twice a yearThirty days from the mailing of the bill

Your actual bill spells out the payment deadline and the abatement deadline. Even when a mortgage company pays through escrow, getting the payment in on time remains your job.

How to apply for an abatement

File an abatement application with your local board of assessors on the approved form, on or before the due date of the first installment of the actual tax bill. In quarterly municipalities that date is generally February 1, and in twice-a-year municipalities it is generally 30 days after the bill is mailed.

  • Pick up the form at the local assessors' office.
  • An abatement is a reduction in tax, usually granted when you can show fair cash value is lower than the assessed value. It can also be granted for an exemption or an improper classification.
  • Fair cash value means what an informed buyer and seller would agree to in an open sale where neither is pressured.
  • A mailed application is treated as filed on its postmark date, whether it went by the Postal Service or an approved carrier.

The assessors then get three months to respond. They may deny the request, grant all or part of it, or let it sit, and written notice is due within ten days of any action. If they do nothing, the application is deemed denied after three calendar months, not 90 days.

Appealing to the Appellate Tax Board

File with the Appellate Tax Board within three months of the assessors' action, or within three months of the deemed denial if they never acted. When the notice shows two dates, count from the date of action, not the mailing date.

Three requirements are jurisdictional, meaning the board cannot hear the case without them: timely payment of the tax, a timely abatement application on the approved form, and a timely appeal. No exceptions can be made. There is one narrow relief on payment: the board can still hear an appeal if the tax due for the year is $5,000 or less, or if you paid at least the average tax of one of the three prior years.

  • The filing fee depends on assessed value under the board's Schedule of Entry Fees.
  • Most single-family appeals use the informal procedure, which waives most further appeal rights.
  • It usually takes four months to a year to get a hearing, most single-family hearings last one to two hours, and a decision arrives within roughly three months.

What you must prove at the hearing

You carry the burden. A tax assessment is presumed valid, so you must show that the fair cash value of your house is below the assessed value as of the January 1 valuation date. Saying that the tax went up 20% generally does not succeed.

Bring a detailed description of the house and a copy of the assessors' record card. Add sales of similar homes close in type, location, size, timing and condition, adjusted for any differences. You may also use comparable assessments or hire an expert appraiser. Documents must reach the board and the other side at least seven days before the hearing.

There is one exception to the presumption. If the board set a value for one year and assessors raise it in either of the next two fiscal years, the burden shifts to the assessors to justify the increase.

When property tax goes unpaid

Skipped property tax, or unpaid water and sewer charges, turns into a lien, and the municipality can end up taking the house. Once a bill is 30 days late it can send a demand. Ignore that demand for 14 days and it can record a tax taking at the Registry of Deeds.

  • After a waiting period of six or twelve months, whoever holds the tax title may start a foreclosure case in the Land Court.
  • A private party can become the tax title owner, for example by buying bundled tax bills or winning an auction.
  • You may answer the complaint and request a hearing. There you can offer to pay off the full balance or propose installments.
  • Miss the payoff date the judge sets and a foreclosure judgment can follow, which cuts off any chance of getting the property back.

If the house was worth more than the debt, a foreclosed owner may be able to claim the difference. It is far easier to settle a tax taking early, before the Land Court gets involved.

Selling with taxes owed

Once a tax taking is recorded, it clouds the title and has to be cleared before the sale can close cleanly. Paying everything owed ends the town's claim if you do it before a final foreclosure judgment. Your closing attorney can explain how unpaid tax gets handled at closing.

Ask the collector's office for a payoff figure before you list. Look over the assessors' record for mistakes, and note any abatement deadline that could fall after you sell. What happens to a pending abatement once the house changes hands is something to ask the assessors and your attorney. A cash buyer can often close with the payoff built into the settlement, though the lien still has to be cleared that day.

Frequently asked questions

What is the deadline to file a Massachusetts property tax abatement?

The cutoff is the first installment due date printed on your real tax bill. Quarterly towns usually land on February 1, and twice-a-year towns run about 30 days from mailing. Your bill states the exact date.

How long do assessors have to decide an abatement?

Three months. Silence for three calendar months counts as a denial, and that starts a three-month window to appeal to the Appellate Tax Board.

Do I have to pay the tax while I appeal?

Generally yes. The Appellate Tax Board needs the tax paid on time to have jurisdiction, with limited exceptions when the tax is $5,000 or less or you paid the average of a prior year.

What does Proposition 2½ limit?

It limits the total levy a municipality can raise. The levy cannot exceed 2.5% of total assessed value, and it can rise by 2.5% of the prior levy limit plus new growth unless voters approve more.

Can the city take my house for unpaid property tax?

Yes, in the end. A demand, then 14 days, then a recorded tax taking, and a Land Court foreclosure can follow. Paying all taxes, interest and fees before final judgment lets you redeem.

What the homestead exemption is

The Massachusetts homestead exemption protects equity in your primary home from most creditors, up to a set dollar amount. It is set out in G.L. c. 188 and comes in two forms: an automatic one and a declared one.

It is not a discount on the yearly property tax bill. Tax exemptions, deferrals and abatements are a separate matter handled through the local board of assessors. This page covers only the creditor protection under chapter 188.

How much equity is protected?

The automatic exemption protects $125,000 of equity with no filing, and a recorded declaration raises the protection to $1,000,000. Both figures come from section 1 of the chapter.

Type of homesteadAmount protectedHow it arises
Automatic$125,000Exists for the owner and family who live in the home or intend to, with no filing (section 4)
Declared$1,000,000Created by a written declaration that is recorded (section 5)
Declared by an elderly or disabled ownerUp to $1,000,000 per personOwner is 62 or older, or disabled; a separate declaration under section 2

When a home is owned as joint tenants or tenants by the entirety, the exemption stays whole and unallocated, and the owners together cannot exceed the cap. Where owners are tenants in common or trust beneficiaries, the automatic exemption is divided by ownership share, and the declared exemption is divided among those who live in the home as a principal residence.

Which properties qualify

The statute defines a home broadly, so most owner-occupied residences qualify. A protected home can be any of these, along with the land and accessory structures that go with it:

  • A single-family house.
  • A two- to four-family dwelling.
  • A manufactured home.
  • A residential condominium unit.
  • A residential cooperative unit.

It must be a principal residence, meaning the place where the owner and family live or intend to live as their main dwelling. No person can hold rights in more than one principal residence. Family counts a spouse and any minor child, and the statute sets "minor child" at age 21 and under.

A federal bankruptcy court decision also found that using part of a property for business does not by itself remove homestead protection.

How to file a declaration of homestead

Sign a written declaration and record it at the Registry of Deeds for the county where the home sits. Section 5 sets what it must contain.

  • Each owner who is to benefit signs and acknowledges it under penalty of perjury.
  • It identifies each owner and any non-titled spouse.
  • It states that each person named lives in the home or intends to as a principal residence.
  • If a married couple co-owns the home as the principal residence of both, both spouses sign.
  • If the home is in a trust, only the trustee signs.
  • It cannot be created inside the deed that gives the owner title.
  • It should state whether anyone named may be a servicemember, though leaving that out does not void it.

The state filing fee is $35, and a county registry may add its own charge. The Norfolk County Registry of Deeds, for example, charges $36 for a declaration of homestead on recorded land, which includes a $1 mailing cost, and $35 on the Land Court side. You can file by mail with notarized signatures and a check.

Owners over 62 or with a disability

An elderly person is someone 62 or older. A disabled person is someone with a permanent impairment that would meet Supplemental Security Income standards. Either can record a separate declaration under section 2.

A disabled owner must record proof with the declaration: an original or certified Social Security Administration disability award letter, or a letter from a registered physician certifying that the federal standard is met. Each person benefited under section 2 gets the declared amount in full, without sharing it among other owners, and separate declarations under sections 2 and 3 can sit on the same home.

What happens to the homestead when you sell

A sale ends the homestead on the house but not the protection for the money. Section 10 lists nine ways a homestead terminates, and a deed is the most common one for sellers.

  • A deed to a non-family member, signed by the owner and by any non-owner spouse or former spouse who lives in the home.
  • A recorded release signed and acknowledged by the owner and that spouse.
  • Abandonment of the home as a principal residence, which ends the rights of the person who left.
  • A new declaration on a different property by the same owner.
  • A deed that states the grantor is unmarried or that the property is not the grantor's home.
  • A divorce judgment that requires conveying the home to the other spouse.

Under section 11, sale proceeds stay protected until you buy another home to live in or one year after the sale, whichever comes first. After fire or other casualty damage, protection lasts until repairs are done, another home is acquired, or two years pass, whichever comes first. Living in a trailer or other temporary housing does not count as establishing a principal residence.

Mortgages and refinancing

Mortgages are treated separately from creditor claims. Section 8 of the chapter deals with prior mortgages and liens, and section 9 with subordination of the homestead to a mortgage signed by all owners. Section 10 adds that nothing in a mortgage or its documents ends a homestead, apart from that subordination. Section 4 allows the automatic exemption to be subordinated to a new loan or line of credit only if the loan is under $20,000, not secured by a recorded document, and signed by all record owners and non-titled spouses with a plain-language waiver.

You do not have to file a declaration again after refinancing, and both spouses may file. A 2021 Appeals Court decision allows a creditor to levy on an execution and then hold off collecting until the homestead lapses or the homeowner's equity exceeds the protected amount. So a judgment can still be waiting when a protected home is sold. Ask the title company or attorney what appears in the record.

What a seller should check before closing

Confirm whether a declaration is on record, and who signed it, before you accept a closing date. The Secretary of the Commonwealth keeps a list of registries you can use to look it up.

  • Search the property at the registry to see whether a declaration or release is recorded.
  • Find out whether a spouse or former spouse who lives in the home needs to sign the deed or a release.
  • Ask whether any judgment lien or tax lien must be paid at closing.
  • Keep proceeds in a way an attorney can explain, because section 11 protection ends one year after the sale unless a new home is bought sooner.

Homes held in trust or owned by several people can involve more signers, so have a real estate attorney read the paperwork first. If the house is going to a cash buyer, the same checks apply, and a clean search up front keeps the closing date from slipping.

Frequently asked questions

Is the Massachusetts homestead automatic?

Yes, to a degree. Chapter 188, section 4 gives an automatic exemption of $125,000 with no filing, as long as the owner and family live in the home or intend to. Recording a declaration raises the protected amount to $1,000,000.

Does the homestead exemption lower my property tax bill?

No. Chapter 188 protects home equity from creditors. Property tax exemptions and abatements are a separate topic handled by your local board of assessors.

How much does it cost to file a declaration of homestead?

The state fee is $35, and a registry may add its own charge. Norfolk County charges $36 for recorded land, which includes a $1 mailing cost.

Do I have to refile after refinancing?

No. There is no need to file the declaration again after a refinance.

What happens if I sell and buy another home?

Sale proceeds stay protected until you acquire another home to live in or one year after the sale, whichever comes first, under section 11.

Who has to file a Massachusetts estate tax return

The personal representative must file Form M-706 when the estate is large enough. For deaths on or after January 1, 2023, that means a gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts above $2,000,000. For deaths from 2006 through 2022 the trigger was $1,000,000. Changes in federal estate tax law after December 31, 2000 have no effect on the Massachusetts tax.

People who didn't live here are covered too. A nonresident who owned or transferred Massachusetts real estate or tangible property has the same filing test, measured against the total worldwide estate, and must send Form M-NRA with the return.

RequirementRule
Filing threshold, deaths from 2023Gross estate over $2,000,000
Filing threshold, deaths 2006 to 2022Gross estate over $1,000,000
Credit, deaths from 2023$99,600
Return and payment dueNine months after death
Late filing penalty1% per month, up to 25%
Late payment penalty1% per month, up to 25%
Estate Tax Unit phone(617) 887-6930

How the tax is calculated

The state computes its tax from the old federal credit for state death taxes, using the Internal Revenue Code as it stood on December 31, 2000, and then subtracts a $99,600 credit. It is a transfer tax on the value of the estate before distribution to any beneficiary.

The computation turns on the federal Table B. The adjusted taxable estate is the taxable estate less $60,000, and there is no credit when that figure is $40,000 or less. Marginal rates in the table run from 0.8 percent up to 16 percent.

Two details affect real estate directly:

  • For deaths on or after August 1, 2025, the value of real and tangible property located outside Massachusetts comes out of a resident's computation.
  • Massachusetts QTIP assets claimed on a predeceased spouse's return are added back, and the steps for deaths between January 1, 2023 and July 31, 2025 follow a separate set of FAQs.

The final amount can't fall below zero. For a real number on a specific estate, ask the Department of Revenue or an estate attorney.

The estate lien and your sale

A lien automatically arises at death on all real estate the decedent owned, either alone or jointly, and it can stand in the way of a clean sale. Failing to file Form M-706 blocks the Certificate Releasing Massachusetts Estate Lien, and a release of lien is necessary to obtain clear title and to sell or transfer the real estate.

When the return must be filed, the certificate is needed for several kinds of real estate:

  • Property owned jointly or as tenants by the entirety.
  • Real estate held in trust.
  • Other real estate outside the probate inventory but included in the gross estate.

It can also be required for probate real estate if a sale is pending and no closing letter has been issued. If the return was already filed, send a copy of the purchase and sale agreement or mortgage commitment to speed up the certificate.

Estates below the threshold

The personal representative signs an affidavit and records it at the registry of deeds to release the lien. The affidavit must be made under the pains and penalties of perjury and must accurately state that the gross estate does not require a Massachusetts estate tax filing. That rule applies to estates of decedents dying on or after January 1, 1997.

Ask the estate's attorney or the registry what form it accepts, since blank affidavits for the registry of deeds come from those offices.

Can the estate sell before the nine-month deadline?

Yes, an estate can sell before the return is due, and there is a form for it. If a sale or mortgage is happening sooner than nine months after death, or later than nine months while an approved extension is running, the estate can file Form M-4422, Application for Certificate Releasing Massachusetts Estate Tax Lien, through MassTaxConnect.

The application needs an executed purchase and sale agreement or mortgage commitment, plus these attachments:

  • An attested copy of the deed.
  • A copy of the purchase and sale agreement or mortgage commitment.
  • A copy of the letter of authority or the trust document.
  • Payment of the estimated tax due.
  • A copy of the death certificate.

The full Form M-706 is still due within nine months of death or within the extension. Filing and paying through MassTaxConnect speeds up the closing letter and the lien release, while mailed returns to P.O. Box 7023, Boston, MA 02204 can delay both.

Extensions and penalties

Every estate return gets an automatic six-month extension to file if at least 80 percent of the tax finally due is paid by the nine-month date. If the 80 percent is missed, the extension is void and the late filing penalty can apply, and interest runs on unpaid tax from the original due date either way.

A separate extension of time to pay is available on Form M-4768 for undue hardship or reasonable cause. Each request covers up to six months, and up to three years from the original due date can be granted in total. Interest keeps accruing during that time. The interest rate changes each quarter, so call the Department of Revenue contact center at (617) 887-6367 or (800) 392-6089 in Massachusetts for the current figure.

The personal representative can be held personally liable for tax shown on the return that isn't paid. Ask an attorney before distributing money to heirs.

What heirs owe and what a cash sale changes

This is a tax on the estate itself, not a tax that each heir pays separately on receiving a share. If you think another state tax applies to your situation, ask the Department of Revenue directly.

A cash sale doesn't remove the lien rules. What it does is shorten the time a house sits while the estate sorts out paperwork. If you are the personal representative of a Massachusetts estate and the house needs repairs, we can look at it as-is, and the estate's attorney handles the lien release or the recorded affidavit.

Before the closing, line up the death certificate, the letter of authority, the signed purchase and sale agreement and either the certificate of release or the recorded affidavit. The title company will ask for each one. Our probate page covers the court steps, and our capital gains page covers the income tax side of the sale.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Massachusetts estate tax exemption in 2026?

A Massachusetts estate tax return is required when the gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts exceeds $2,000,000, for deaths on or after January 1, 2023. Estates also receive a $99,600 credit.

When is the Massachusetts estate tax due?

Nine months after the date of death. An automatic six-month extension to file applies if at least 80 percent of the tax is paid by the nine-month date.

Do I need a lien release to sell an inherited house in Massachusetts?

If the estate is over the threshold, yes in many cases. A Certificate Releasing Massachusetts Estate Lien is needed to obtain clear title. Smaller estates use a recorded affidavit that the gross estate does not require a filing.

Can I sell the house before filing the estate tax return?

Yes. If a purchase and sale agreement is signed, the estate can apply on Form M-4422 for the certificate releasing the lien. A completed Form M-706 is still due within nine months or the extension period.

Who do I call with questions about the Massachusetts estate tax?

Call the Estate Tax Unit at (617) 887-6930. For other ways to reach the Department of Revenue, call the contact center at (617) 887-6367, weekdays 9 a.m. to 4 p.m.

Steps of an eviction once the notice runs out

When the days on the notice to quit are up, the landlord can file a summary process case. Only a judge's order can end the tenancy. The sequence runs like this.

  1. The landlord fills out a summons and complaint and hires a sheriff or constable to deliver it to the tenant.
  2. The landlord files the papers in a District Court or a Housing Court.
  3. The tenant may file a written answer, which costs nothing.
  4. The parties go to court, where the case is dismissed, settled by agreement, or tried.
  5. If the landlord wins, the judge may issue an execution, the order that lets the move-out go forward.
  6. A sheriff or constable carries out the removal after written notice.

No total timeline is promised anywhere. Each step depends on the court calendar, so if you are planning a sale, treat any single estimate with caution.

District Court or Housing Court?

Either one can hear the case. Landlords can file in a District Court or a Housing Court, and Housing Courts know housing law better than district or superior court judges do.

A tenant can ask to transfer a case into Housing Court, though not the other way around. In Housing Court the first appearance is usually aimed at settling the dispute through mediation, and the case goes to trial only if that fails. Expect more than one court date, and bring any lease, rent ledger and written messages with the tenant to each one.

State law organizes these courts by chapter. Chapter 185A covers the Housing Court of the City of Boston, chapter 185B covers the Housing Court of the County of Hampden, and chapter 185C covers the statewide Housing Court Department. Which court serves a given town depends on where the house sits, so the clerk's office is the place to confirm.

What happens after a judge rules for the landlord?

A ruling for the landlord starts a short clock. It does not mean an immediate move-out.

StepTimeDetail
Appeal window10 daysCounted from the date the clerk's office enters judgment
Earliest removal11 days after the final decisionThe landlord can then hire a sheriff or constable
Written notice before removal2 daysWeekends and holidays not counted; the notice names the storage facility
Removal hoursMonday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.Not on a holiday
Window to use the execution3 monthsFrom the court decision
Stay of executionUp to 6 monthsUp to a year for elderly or disabled tenants

A tenant who wants to appeal may first have to pay money owed, such as back rent, though the court can be asked to waive that when it is unaffordable.

A tenant can also ask the judge for a stay of execution, which postpones the move. A judge may grant one when the eviction is not the tenant's fault or the tenant shows that no good place to live can be found yet. Most stays last up to six months.

Can paying the rent stop an eviction after judgment?

Yes, in one situation. The landlord cannot move the tenant out when the eviction is based on nonpayment, the tenant pays all the rent due before the execution is used, and the landlord accepts the payment.

All three conditions must hold together. Because it depends on the landlord accepting the money, a written agreement is the safer way to record what both sides agreed. A pending RAFT application also blocks an eviction, and the tenant should tell the court if one has been filed.

Removal day: belongings and the house

If the tenant has not left, the sheriff or constable takes the belongings to an approved storage facility, and the tenant can be charged for moving and storage. The written notice must give the storage address.

  • A storage facility that holds belongings for six months without payment is allowed to sell them.
  • Only a sheriff or constable can carry out the removal, and only after the 11-day wait.
  • A landlord who locks the tenant out without a judge's order can face penalties under G.L. c. 186, section 14.
  • A tenant who leaves voluntarily before removal avoids the moving and storage fees.

The house is not truly vacant until the removal is complete and you have walked the property. A buyer who inspects before closing will see whatever condition the tenant left it in, so plan time for cleanup and repairs before photos and showings.

If the tenant moves out owing money

A landlord can still sue for unpaid rent or other damages after the tenant leaves, in a civil case or in small claims. Small claims generally caps recovery at $7,000. A $9,000 debt would be cut to $7,000 and the other $2,000 waived.

Talk to a lawyer before filing a civil action for damages. One special rule sits in G.L. c. 139, section 19: if illegal drugs were found in the unit, the landlord can ask for a speedy trial, and the court may order judgment and execution to issue immediately after trial or default.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Massachusetts houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How an eviction case affects a house sale

An eviction case adds waiting time and paperwork to a sale, and it can follow the people involved for years. A case can appear on a tenant's housing record and a money judgment can affect credit, though a tenant may ask to seal the record or file a satisfaction of judgment once paid.

For owners, the practical effects tend to be these:

  • Possession cannot be promised on a fixed date until the court process and the removal are done.
  • A landlord has three months to use an execution, so timing matters if the house is under contract.
  • A tenant in the middle of a case may stay until removal, which affects showings and inspections.
  • Back rent and court costs are separate from the sale and are not wiped out by it.

Owners who would rather skip the court calendar sometimes sell with the tenant in place, or negotiate a move-out date in writing. A cash buyer who takes the house as it stands avoids waiting on a vacant unit. A real estate attorney can say which path fits a particular lease or tenancy at will.

Free help for landlords and tenants

The state runs several free resources. The Community Mediation Centers offer free pre-court mediation, the Court Service Centers help court users without lawyers regardless of income or immigration status, and the Legal Resource Finder points to legal aid programs.

Tenants behind on rent can apply to RAFT through their regional administering agency. Landlords can start an application too, which helps because the program needs the landlord's cooperation. For a seller with a case in progress, a settled payment plan through RAFT can clear the way to a normal closing faster than a trial.

Frequently asked questions

How long does an eviction take in Massachusetts?

There is no fixed total, because it depends on the notice period, the court calendar and the time for appeal and removal. After judgment, the earliest removal is 11 days after the final decision.

Can a landlord evict a tenant without going to court in Massachusetts?

No. A landlord cannot lock a tenant out or remove them without a judge's order, and doing so can bring penalties under G.L. c. 186, section 14.

How long does a landlord have to use an execution?

Three months from the court decision. The execution is only valid for that window.

Can a tenant be evicted while a RAFT application is pending?

No. A tenant cannot be evicted while a RAFT application is pending and should tell the court about it.

Who serves the eviction papers?

An authorized constable or sheriff must serve the summons and complaint. The landlord cannot serve them personally.

What a quitclaim deed does

A Massachusetts quitclaim deed passes along whatever interest the grantor can lawfully convey. Chapter 183, section 2 of the General Laws says a deed of quitclaim and release is enough to convey all the estate that could lawfully be conveyed by a deed of bargain and sale.

The statute also defines the covenants that go with it. Quitclaim covenants, also called limited covenants, mean the grantor promises the property is free of encumbrances made by the grantor, and will defend the title against claims by, through or under the grantor, but against no one else. That is narrower than a promise about the whole history of the title.

Quitclaim deed versus warranty deed

The difference is how far the grantor's promises reach. A quitclaim deed with quitclaim covenants limits the guarantee to the grantor's own acts. Massachusetts also provides a statutory form for a warranty deed with broader warranty covenants.

CovenantWhat the grantor promises under M.G.L. c. 183, section 17
Free of encumbrancesOnly those made by the grantor
Defends title againstClaims by, through or under the grantor
Claims from earlier ownersNot covered

A buyer who accepts a quitclaim deed is relying on the grantor's own acts only, so ask your closing attorney what extra title work makes sense.

What a deed must contain to be recorded

Section 6 of chapter 183 sets two musts for any deed sent in for recording. It has to show the buyer's full name, home and mailing address, and it has to recite the full consideration. Those items can also be endorsed on the deed.

  • Full consideration is the whole price, with no subtraction for mortgages or liens the buyer takes on or that stay on the land.
  • When the deal is not for a set amount of money, the deed describes what was given instead.
  • These recitals become part of the recorded deed.
  • A register of deeds must turn away a deed that leaves them out, even though the deed itself stays valid.

Even a gift between relatives needs a stated consideration. A deed missing these details can be refused at the counter, and that can push back a closing date.

Where a Massachusetts deed is recorded

The county Registry of Deeds is where deeds go, and the state runs two title systems side by side. Recorded land is filed with the registry itself. Registered land sits with the Land Court, in districts housed inside the registries.

Roughly 80 to 90 percent of properties are recorded land. Each filing gets a book and page number and shows up online at masslandrecords.com. Registered land has a Certificate of Title that counts as a Land Court decree, so its deeds are handled on the Land Court side.

Find out which system covers your property before you sign anything. Registry staff can answer in minutes, or you can read the current deed at masslandrecords.com.

The deeds excise tax

The base rate in the statute is $2 for each $500, or fraction, of consideration, and $1.50 in Barnstable County. Chapter 64D, section 1 exempts an instrument given to secure a debt, and any deed where the commonwealth, a city or town, or the United States is a party.

Registries post the amount they actually collect. Norfolk County shows $2.28 for each $500 and any fraction of the consideration stated on the deed, with a worked case: $155,000 of consideration means $706.80. Below $100 of consideration, no excise tax is due.

  • Pay the tax when the deed is recorded.
  • Norfolk wants it on its own attorney's check or bank check.
  • Recording fees go on a second check.

Call the registry for your county's current rate and payment rules before closing day.

Recording fees

Each registry sets its own fees. At Norfolk, a deed costs $156 on recorded land, which includes a $1 mailing cost, and $155 on the Land Court side. A declaration of homestead is $36 and a declaration of trust is $256.

Electronic filings skip the $1 postage and return charge as of July 1, 2025. A document that must go on both the Land Court and registry sides needs one check for each. Because other counties post different schedules, ask the registry that will record your deed for its numbers, and bring the payment types it accepts.

Home inspections and attorneys at closing

Under 760 CMR 74, sellers of certain residential properties may not make an offer depend on the buyer giving up a home inspection, and may not take offers from buyers who have said they plan to waive one. Whether your sale falls under it depends on the property.

A Supreme Judicial Court decision also requires an attorney to take a real part in lender closings. Whatever deed you use, plan on an attorney being involved, and ask yours early which documents they will draft.

Does a quitclaim deed fix title problems?

No. The deed hands over whatever the grantor has, and it cannot repair a defect that is already there. It will not reveal liens, tax takings or probate gaps either, so have an attorney decide what title work is needed.

Attorneys are a normal part of Massachusetts sales, by law and by habit. On some purchase money mortgages for homes of up to four families, the lender's attorney must certify title under M.G.L. c. 93, section 70.

  • Check for unpaid property tax or a recorded tax taking.
  • Work out who has to sign, such as a co-owner or an estate representative.
  • Find out whether the land is recorded or registered, because that decides where the deed is filed.
  • Review the deed form with a Massachusetts attorney.

Steps from signing to recording

The grantor signs the deed in front of a notary, and the signed original goes to whoever handles the closing. That person takes it to the registry after the funds move, along with one check for the excise tax and another for the recording fees. The registry stamps the deed with a book and page number once it is accepted.

As the seller, ask for a copy of the recorded deed afterward. If the registry rejects the deed for a missing address or recital, the fix is usually quick, but it can hold up the closing for a day or more.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

When a quitclaim deed works for a sale

It works when the grantor holds clear title and the buyer is comfortable with limited covenants and a title search. It is a common instrument for sales and for family transfers.

Selling a one or two family home also means getting a smoke and carbon monoxide alarm certificate of compliance from the local fire department. Call them once a closing date is set. When the owner has died, the deed must be signed by a personal representative who has authority to sell, and a lawyer should confirm the steps before a quitclaim deed is used to move the house out of an estate.

A cash buyer who accepts limited covenants can close quickly on a quitclaim deed, as long as the title search comes back clean.

Frequently asked questions

Is a quitclaim deed valid in Massachusetts?

Yes. Under chapter 183, section 2, a deed of quitclaim and release conveys everything the grantor could lawfully pass by a bargain and sale deed.

What does the grantee information on a deed have to include?

The buyer's full name, home and mailing address, plus the full consideration. A register of deeds may refuse a deed without them.

How is the Massachusetts deeds excise tax figured?

The statute's base is $2 per $500 of consideration, while the Norfolk County Registry collects $2.28 per $500. Ask the registry where you record for today's rate.

Where is a quitclaim deed recorded?

At the county Registry of Deeds, on the recorded land side or the Land Court side depending on how the property is titled. Recorded documents get a book and page number.

Where can I look up my deed online?

At masslandrecords.com, which provides access to registry records from across the state.

Transfer on death deeds in Massachusetts

Do not count on a transfer on death deed to pass a Massachusetts house until a Massachusetts attorney confirms in writing that it works and how it is recorded. A deed meant to pass a house at death is not something to guess about.

The state's probate code does touch the subject. G.L. c. 190B, section 6-101 says a provision for a nonprobate transfer on death in a long list of instruments is nontestamentary. The list includes insurance policies, accounts, securities, trusts, and a conveyance or deed of gift, along with any other written instrument effective as a contract, gift, conveyance or trust.

That section is general. It tells you such provisions are not wills, but it does not by itself create a specific deed form for a house. A separate chapter 201E, the Uniform Transfer on Death Security Registration Act, concerns securities rather than land.

What happens to a house when the owner dies?

It depends on how title is held. Whether an estate has to be probated turns on how the decedent's property is titled at death.

Some property passes directly by law and stays out of the probate estate. Jointly held property with a right of survivorship goes to the surviving owner. Proceeds from a life insurance policy or an account that names a beneficiary go to that beneficiary. Property held in a trust created by the decedent is handled under the trust.

Typically you must probate the estate if you need to change the title of real estate that is only in the decedent's name without any right of survivorship. A house titled solely to the person who died is the standard case, and it is why this matters to heirs who want to sell.

  • Sole owner, no survivorship, no trust: probate is usually needed to change title.
  • Joint owners with survivorship: the survivor takes by law.
  • House held in the decedent's trust: the trust terms and trustee control.

Types of probate

Massachusetts has three types of probate and a simplified process called voluntary administration. Which one fits depends on the will, the heirs and whether the estate includes land.

ProcessWhat it involves
Informal probateAdministrative, handled by a Massachusetts Uniform Probate Code magistrate with no hearings. A magistrate can issue an informal order as early as 7 days after death. Requires the original will, the official death certificate, and the identity and location of all heirs and devisees.
Formal probateTypically heard by a judge and may involve hearings. Used to object to an informal probate, when the will is a copy or has handwritten changes, when its terms are unclear, or when supervised administration is needed.
Late and limited formal probateFor deaths on or after March 31, 2012, when no proceeding happened within 3 years and only confirmation of ownership of probate assets is needed. The personal representative cannot get a license to sell the decedent's real estate.
Voluntary administrationFor estates that consist entirely of personal property worth $25,000 or less, excluding a car, with no real estate.

A house takes an estate out of voluntary administration, since that process is meant for an estate with few assets and no real estate.

Is there a deadline to probate an estate?

The general rule is three years from the date of death. An estate has to be probated within 3 years of when the decedent died.

The deadline does not apply to a voluntary administration, to determining heirs, or to an ancillary proceeding. If the decedent died on or after March 31, 2012 and nothing was filed within the three years, a late and limited formal probate may be available, and in some cases voluntary administration too if its criteria are met.

That late route has a catch for anyone hoping to sell. A late and limited personal representative cannot get a license to sell real estate, so an heir who waited past three years may have a harder path to a clean sale than one who started early. Talk to a probate attorney about your timeline.

  • Within 3 years: full set of probate options available.
  • After 3 years: late and limited formal probate for deaths on or after March 31, 2012.
  • Voluntary administration: at least 30 days must separate the date of death from filing, and the estate must meet the personal property limit.

Who can serve as personal representative?

A person with legal priority, usually the executor named in the will. If the decedent left a will, priority goes to the person named in it as personal representative or executor.

If there was no will, the surviving spouse has priority. If the decedent was not married when they died, the decedent's heirs have priority. A qualified person with priority has the right to be appointed over anyone else.

The personal representative collects, manages and transfers estate property to the devisees or heirs. When a house is part of the estate, this is also the person who signs the sale paperwork, subject to whatever authority the court gives. Informal probate requires that the person to be appointed has priority.

Recording when an inherited house is sold

A sale deed from the estate or its representative is recorded at the registry of deeds like any other. G.L. c. 183, section 4 provides that a conveyance of a fee simple estate is not valid against most outside parties unless recorded in the registry for the county or district where the land lies.

Ask your probate attorney what proof of authority the registry for your county requires from the person signing for the seller. Chapter 202 of the General Laws, which covers sales, mortgages and leases of real estate by executors, administrators, guardians and conservators, is the part of the code to ask about.

  • Probate the estate if the house was in the decedent's sole name.
  • Confirm the personal representative's authority to sell.
  • Close with an attorney and record the deed at the registry for the property's county.

Heirs who inherit a house they do not want to keep can sell it as-is. Cash Home Buyers can give an offer on an inherited Massachusetts house, and your attorney should confirm the estate paperwork is in order before closing.

Questions to ask a Massachusetts attorney

Ask whether any deed on your property transfers it at death, who the sole owner is, and what process the estate would need. Bring your current deed and any trust or will.

  • How is title held on my house today?
  • If I die, would the house need probate?
  • Would a trust or joint ownership with survivorship fit my family and my goals?
  • If a relative died recently, which probate type applies and by when?

For an heir who is already holding a house, the answers decide the order of steps: probate first, then authority to sell, then the closing and recording. Skipping ahead to a listing before the representative has authority tends to cost time.

Frequently asked questions

What is a transfer on death deed?

It is a deed that names who receives property when the owner dies. Check with a Massachusetts attorney before relying on one for a house.

Does a house always go through probate in Massachusetts?

No. It depends on how the property is titled. Jointly held property with survivorship, property in a trust, and accounts naming beneficiaries can pass outside probate.

What is the deadline to probate an estate in Massachusetts?

The general rule is 3 years from the date of death. A late and limited formal probate may be available for deaths on or after March 31, 2012, but that route cannot license a sale of real estate.

Can voluntary administration be used for an estate with a house?

No. It is meant for estates with no real estate and personal property worth $25,000 or less, excluding a car.

How fast can informal probate start?

A magistrate can issue an informal order as early as 7 days after death, if you have the original will, the death certificate and the identity of all heirs and devisees.

Types of probate in Massachusetts

Massachusetts has three types of probate plus a simplified process called voluntary administration. The Probate and Family Court sorts them into informal probate, formal probate, and late and limited formal probate.

TypeWho decidesMain feature
Informal probateA Massachusetts Uniform Probate Code magistrateAdministrative, no hearings
Formal probateUsually a judgeOne or more court hearings
Late and limited formal probateThe courtFor estates with no proceeding within 3 years
Voluntary administrationThe court, simplifiedSmall estate, no real estate

If your family wants to sell an inherited house, the type of proceeding decides how soon a sale can close, so pick the right one early.

When informal probate works

Informal probate is available only if you meet every requirement, and it can be faster. A magistrate can issue an informal order as early as 7 days after the death.

  • You have the original will, if there is one, and the official death certificate.
  • You know the identity and location of all heirs and devisees.
  • The person to be appointed personal representative has priority for appointment.
  • Any incapacitated or minor spouse, heir or devisee is represented by a conservator or a guardian who is not the person filing.
  • The court has not required supervised administration.
  • No judge needs to sign an order or final decree.

Written notice must reach the people entitled to it at least 7 days before you file. The filing fee for an informal petition is $375, plus a $15 surcharge. You can file online, by mail or in person in the county where the decedent lived. Once the court accepts the petition, post a publication notice within 30 days in a newspaper the register designates.

When you need formal probate

File a formal probate when informal probate is not available or when a judge must act. Several of the reasons come up often for families holding a house.

  • Someone objects to an informal probate.
  • The will is a copy, or has handwritten words added or crossed out.
  • The terms of the will are unclear.
  • A special personal representative is needed.
  • An incapacitated person or minor heir needs representation.
  • The person asking to serve does not have priority, or is a creditor or public administrator.

Formal matters usually involve one or more hearings before a judge, so plan for a longer timeline than with informal probate. Supervised administration, where the court approves each step, is possible but not commonly required.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Massachusetts house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Who can sell a house the decedent owned?

A personal representative can sell estate real estate to an arm's-length third party, but only if one of two conditions is met. Section 3-715 of the Massachusetts Uniform Probate Code, chapter 190B, covers this power, and it applies whether the representative was appointed formally or informally.

  • If the person died without a will, a license to sell must have been issued under chapter 202.
  • If the person died with a will, either the will, probated formally or informally, gave the representative power to sell that real estate, or a chapter 202 license has been issued.

When those conditions are met, the sale is conclusive even if someone later contests the informal probate. Keep the appointment and the will language or license together so your closing attorney can review them.

Late and limited appointments cannot sell a house

A personal representative appointed in a late and limited formal probate cannot get a license to sell the decedent's real estate. That appointment can only confirm ownership of probate assets in the successors and pay administration expenses.

This type applies when the decedent died on or after March 31, 2012, no original estate proceeding happened within 3 years of the death, and you only need a formal proceeding to confirm ownership. If an old house has sat for years and a sale is the goal, you may need a different route, and a probate attorney can tell you which.

If the owner lived outside Massachusetts

File in any Massachusetts county where the decedent had property at death. If the person did not live in Massachusetts, you may also need to file additional forms in the state where they lived.

An ancillary proceeding like this also needs an authenticated copy of the will, if there is one, and of the appointment. If the person lived in Massachusetts, the rule is simpler: file in the county where they lived at death.

You can check a case's status online and file through the court's eFiling system. Contact the Probate and Family Court location for the county before you travel, because accepted payment methods for fees vary.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Massachusetts houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Voluntary administration and houses

Voluntary administration is for estates with few assets and no real estate. It requires a Massachusetts resident decedent whose estate consists entirely of personal property worth $25,000 or less, not counting a car, and at least 30 days since the death.

A house is real estate, so an estate that includes one cannot use this process. Another probate proceeding also cannot be pending. A voluntary personal representative's authority is limited and does not lead to an official court appointment, which is why a house sale calls for one of the other types.

Forms for an informal probate petition

The forms depend on whether there is a will. With a will, file the petition (MPC 150), the surviving spouse, children and heirs form (MPC 162), the devisees form (MPC 163), the original will, a certified death certificate, a notice and return of service (MPC 550), a proposed order (MPC 750) and a publication notice (MPC 551).

Without a will, you file the same petition, heirs form, death certificate and notice, plus a bond (MPC 801). You may need a military affidavit if not every interested party agrees, and proof of any guardianship or conservatorship. The court also offers a checklist for informal probate, MPC 966, which is worth reading before you file.

Selling an inherited house quickly

A sale can close as soon as the personal representative has authority to sell and the title is clear. Heirs who live out of state, or who do not want to repair and clean the house, sometimes choose a buyer who purchases as-is. Hand the appointment and the license or will language to the closing attorney early, so a cash offer does not stall at the title review.

Property tax, utilities and insurance continue during probate, so keep them current to avoid a tax taking. If you are unsure whether you need informal or formal probate, contact the Probate and Family Court in the county where the person lived, or a Massachusetts probate attorney. A call to the court before you pick a petition costs nothing and can save a refiling.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

How soon can a Massachusetts informal probate order be issued?

A magistrate can issue an informal order as early as 7 days after the death, if you meet every requirement. Notice to the people entitled to it must go out at least 7 days before you file.

How much does it cost to file an informal probate in Massachusetts?

The filing fee is $375 plus a $15 surcharge for an informal probate petition. Ask the county court location which forms of payment it accepts.

Can a personal representative sell a house without a license to sell?

Sometimes. If the person died with a will, the sale is covered when the will gave the power to sell that real estate. Without a will, a chapter 202 license is required under section 3-715.

Does voluntary administration work if the decedent owned a house?

No. It is only for estates made up entirely of personal property worth $25,000 or less, not counting a car. A house is real estate, so another type of probate applies.

Which court handles probate in Massachusetts?

The Probate and Family Court. For a Massachusetts resident, you file in the county where the person lived when they died.

Does Massachusetts tax the gain when I sell a house?

Yes. The gain counts as income, though a seller of a main home can often keep much of it out of the calculation. The profit goes on your state return, and the Department of Revenue sets the rate by how long you held the property.

The same return reports everything else you earned that year, so a large sale can sit next to other income near the surtax threshold. Ask a preparer about timing before you sign.

Type of gainMassachusetts rate
Long-term capital gain5.00%
Short-term capital gain8.5%
Long-term gain on collectibles12.00%, with a 50% deduction
Extra surtax, tax year 20264% on income over $1,107,750

A house is not a collectible, so the 12 percent line matters only for items sold alongside a property.

The principal residence exclusion

Massachusetts borrows the federal home-sale exclusion: $250,000 of gain is shielded when you sell your principal residence, and $500,000 when you file a joint return. The state conforms to Internal Revenue Code section 121 and applies it through M.G.L. c. 62, sections 1(c), 1(d) and 2(a).

  • Only a principal residence qualifies. Investment property and second homes don't.
  • The ceiling is $250,000 for a single filer and $500,000 for a joint return.
  • Profit beyond the ceiling is taxed at the rate for your holding period.

Have a tax professional check the federal ownership and use tests before you count on the exclusion. Gather the closing statement, your purchase records and receipts for major improvements so the preparer can work out your gain.

A short checklist helps at the preparer's desk. Bring the closing statement from your purchase, the one from the sale, and proof of the years the house was your main home. Add receipts for a new roof, an addition or a remodeled kitchen. Those raise your basis and shrink the gain. With co-owners, each person reports a share of the gain on a personal return.

Investment houses and rentals

Selling a rental means no principal residence exclusion, so the entire gain faces the 5 percent or 8.5 percent rate. A tenant in the house changes nothing about the rate, which turns on how long you owned it.

Hold the house longer than a year and the lower long-term rate applies. Sell at a year or less and the gain lands in the 8.5 percent group. When the sale falls close to the one-year mark, confirm the dates with a tax adviser, because the rate difference is 3.5 percentage points on every taxable dollar.

Selling costs such as agent commissions and legal fees reduce the gain, so keep every closing document. For a former rental, ask the preparer how past depreciation changes the figure. It starts as a federal question and carries onto the state return. Moving the closing into another calendar year can shift the gain into a lighter income year, which matters near the surtax threshold.

When the tax is due

You pay with your annual return, filed by April 15 for the prior year. A big mid-year sale can also trigger estimated payments.

Estimated installments on Form 1-ES fall in these months:

  • April 15
  • June
  • September
  • January of the following year

An extension buys time to file but not time to pay, and interest runs on whatever is unpaid. It only counts if 80 percent of the liability is paid by the original date, and a payment of $5,000 or more with an extension has to go in electronically. Filing an extension with the IRS doesn't count as a Massachusetts extension. For payment questions, phone the Department of Revenue at (617) 887-6367, or toll free at (800) 392-6089 inside Massachusetts, weekdays from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m.

After a large gain, calculate the estimated payment right away. It is easier to hold back cash from the proceeds than to find it the following April.

Deeds excise is a different tax

Two different taxes touch a sale. Capital gains tax falls on your profit. The deeds excise falls on the price: $2.28 for every $500, less any mortgage the buyer assumes.

A fully excluded gain doesn't erase the excise, which shows up as its own closing line. Your closing attorney can tell you what your deed owes. TIR 19-14 covers surcharge information.

Other steps that affect your net

Several state rules shape the timeline and your costs regardless of the tax result. Lawyers take part in nearly every Massachusetts sale, by law and by long habit. Most properties, 80 to 90 percent, are recorded land with deeds filed at a county Registry of Deeds. The remainder is registered land, backed by a Land Court certificate. You can sign up with the Secretary of the Commonwealth for an email alert when a new document is recorded against your property, and masslandrecords.com is the search site.

Every sale also needs a smoke and carbon monoxide certificate of compliance from the local fire department, which charges a fee. Book that inspection the moment a closing date is set. Expired battery alarms, or any older than ten years, have to be swapped for sealed 10-year photoelectric units with a hush feature.

Property tax is its own bill and has nothing to do with the gain. Boston charges $12.40 per $1,000 of residential value, and Cambridge's FY2027 residential rate is $6.95 per $1,000.

Selling an inherited house

Inheriting the house raises other issues, and the estate lien and release rules can change the closing. See our Massachusetts estate tax page for the $2,000,000 threshold, the $99,600 credit and the release of lien process, and our probate page for the court side.

Ask a Massachusetts tax preparer how the inherited basis works for your return. A house that needs work can sell as-is for cash, so you skip repairs. The smoke and carbon monoxide certificate still applies.

Closing steps for a cash sale run in a simple order. You sign the purchase agreement, the title work gets cleared, and you sign the deed at closing. Afterward, set aside the tax on any taxable gain before you spend the proceeds, and hand your preparer the closing statement for next year's return. If an estate lien or a recorded affidavit is part of the picture, ask the attorney to confirm it is finished before the closing date so nothing delays the funds.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Massachusetts capital gains tax rate on a house?

Long-term gains are taxed at 5.00 percent and short-term gains at 8.5 percent. A 4 percent surtax applies to income over $1,107,750 in tax year 2026.

How much profit can I exclude on my main home in Massachusetts?

Up to $250,000, or $500,000 if you file jointly. Massachusetts conforms to Internal Revenue Code section 121 for this exclusion.

Is there a difference between short-term and long-term gains on a house?

Yes. Gains on assets held one year or less are taxed at 8.5 percent, while long-term gains are taxed at 5.00 percent. The difference is 3.5 percentage points on the taxable amount.

Do I owe the deeds excise even if my gain is excluded?

Yes. The excise is a separate transfer tax of $2.28 per $500 of the price, less any mortgage assumed. Your closing attorney can give the exact amount.

When do I pay Massachusetts tax on the gain?

With your yearly return, due April 15 of the next year. Large gains may require Form 1-ES estimates, and a filing extension doesn't delay payment.

Where a deed gets recorded

A deed to Massachusetts land is recorded at the registry of deeds for the county or registry district where the land lies. That rule comes from G.L. c. 183, section 4. Without recording in that registry, a conveyance of a fee simple estate cannot be enforced against most outside parties.

Three groups are bound regardless: the grantor, the grantor's heirs and devisees, and anyone who actually knew about the deed. Even so, a signed deed should never sit in a drawer. A later buyer, a creditor or an attachment could beat an unrecorded deed in a priority dispute.

Sellers rarely file the deed themselves. After the money changes hands, the closer carries it to the correct registry. That is usually the attorney working for the buyer or the buyer's lender. It still pays to know where it is headed and how to confirm it arrived.

Recorded land and registered land

Massachusetts runs two title systems side by side. Between eighty and ninety percent of Commonwealth properties are recorded land.

Recorded land is the familiar kind. Every document gets a book and page number and can be viewed online. Registered land works differently: a Land Court decree called a Certificate of Title lists the owner, describes the parcel and notes any encumbrances.

Registered land is still handled at the county registry, because the Land Court's registered land districts are housed inside the county registries. It does change what you file. Norfolk County, for example, publishes two columns on its fee schedule, one for recorded land and one for the Land Court side, and a document needing both needs two separate checks.

  • Recorded land: indexed by book and page, searchable online.
  • Registered land: backed by a Land Court Certificate of Title.
  • Unsure which you own: ask the registry or your closing attorney.

What a deed must contain to be accepted

G.L. c. 183, section 6 requires the grantee's full name, residence and post office address on any deed offered for recording, along with a recital of the full consideration.

The consideration is the entire price, with nothing subtracted for liens or encumbrances the buyer assumes or that stay on the property. A deed not given for a set sum of money must describe whatever was given instead. These recitals are recorded along with the deed.

Here is the part that surprises sellers. A missing item does not make the deed invalid, but a register of deeds is barred from accepting it. The deed can be perfectly good between the parties and still bounce at the counter.

  • The buyer's full legal name and mailing address, on the deed or endorsed on it.
  • The price in dollars, figured before any mortgage the buyer takes over is subtracted.

What recording costs

Recording involves two separate items: a registry recording fee and the deeds excise tax. Each registry sets and posts its own fees, so the safest figure is the one on your registry's current schedule.

As one example, the Norfolk County Registry of Deeds fee schedule lists a deed at $156.00 for recorded land and $155.00 on the Land Court side. A mortgage is $206.00, a mortgage discharge is $106.00 per marginal reference, a declaration of homestead is $36.00 and a municipal lien certificate is $81.00. A one dollar postage and return charge applies to documents mailed or recorded in person. Electronic filings skip it as of July 1, 2025.

Document or service at NorfolkRecorded landLand Court side
Deed$156.00$155.00
Mortgage$206.00$205.00
Mortgage discharge$106.00$105.00
Declaration of homestead$36.00$35.00
Copies, per page$1.00$1.00

Another county may charge differently, so get the exact figure from that registry or your attorney.

How the deeds excise tax works

This tax is figured on the price stated in the deed, per $500 or fraction of $500. G.L. c. 64D, section 1 sets the base at $2.00 for each additional $500 or fractional part, and $1.50 in Barnstable County.

It reaches deeds with consideration above one hundred dollars, not counting liens or encumbrances that remain. Exempt are instruments given to secure a debt and deeds where the Commonwealth, a city or town, or the United States or their agencies is a party.

Norfolk County collects $2.28 for each $500 and any fraction, and its worked example puts the tax on a $155,000 deed at $706.80. Pay what your own registry's current schedule says. Norfolk wants an attorney's check or bank check for the tax, apart from the recording fee, and charges nothing when consideration is under $100.

  • The stated price drives the amount, so the consideration on the deed matters.
  • The purchase agreement says who pays, so check with your attorney before signing.
  • Any part of a $500 block counts as a whole block, which means the figure rounds up.

What goes to the registry

Send the original signed deed, the recording fee and the excise tax payment, plus anything else your registry requests.

Lenders and title insurers usually insist on an attorney, so the closing attorney typically handles all of this. In Massachusetts, attorneys are part of real estate sales by law and by custom. The Supreme Judicial Court's decision in Real Estate Bar Association v. National Real Estate Information Services, 459 Mass. 512 (2011), held that a lender's closing requires an attorney's substantive participation.

  • The signed, acknowledged original deed, not a photocopy.
  • The recording fee, by check or electronic payment as the registry directs.
  • The excise tax on its own bank or attorney's check.

Norfolk accepts cash or check for recording and copy fees. A document recorded on both the Land Court and registry sides needs its own check for each.

Checking that your deed was recorded

Look the document up on masslandrecords.com or your registry's own site. You can also sign up for an alert service. Masslandrecords.com is where to find copies of your deed and mortgage too.

The Secretary of the Commonwealth offers a consumer notification service that emails you whenever a new document is recorded against your property. Norfolk County's registry also has a page about deed scams.

The assessors' office is another source. Owners can pull up their deed online next to the property record card used to produce the tax bill. If a recorded deed does not appear after a few days, call the registry and ask your closing attorney to follow up.

Other state rules that touch a sale

Two state rules matter beyond recording. G.L. c. 93, section 70 has the mortgagee's attorney certify title to both the mortgagor and the mortgagee when a purchase money first mortgage is granted on an owner-occupied dwelling for up to four families.

The home inspection waiver regulation, 760 CMR 74, bars sellers of certain residential properties from making an offer depend on a waived inspection, or from taking offers from buyers who plan to waive one. Whether it reaches your sale turns on the property and the buyer, so ask your attorney.

Liens, back taxes and a muddled chain of title tend to surface at recording. Bring them up with your attorney early.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I record a deed in Massachusetts?

At the registry of deeds serving the county or district where the property sits. Recording there is what makes the deed good against most third parties under G.L. c. 183, section 4.

How much is the excise tax when I sell my house?

The tax is a set amount per $500 of the price stated in the deed. The Norfolk County registry collects $2.28 per $500 and shows $706.80 on a $155,000 deed, while G.L. c. 64D, section 1 gives a base of $2 per $500. Check your registry for the current rate.

Can a deed be valid but not accepted for recording?

Yes. A missing grantee address or consideration recital does not affect validity under G.L. c. 183, section 6, but a register of deeds may not accept a deed that lacks them.

Does every Massachusetts property use the same title system?

No. Most properties, an estimated eighty to ninety percent, are recorded land, and the rest are registered land with a Certificate of Title through the Land Court.

How do I get a copy of my recorded deed?

Search masslandrecords.com or ask your registry. Norfolk County lists copies at $1.00 per page, plus a postage charge for copies ordered by mail.
